title: New York Bans Horse-Drawn Carriages Under Romanch's Law, Honouring Indian Teen
excerpt: The City Council voted 40-7 to phase out horse-drawn carriages by June 1, 2028, naming the law for Romanch Mahajan, 18, of Pathankot, who died in June trying to save his mother after a carriage horse bolted in Central Park.
body:
• New York's City Council has passed Romanch's Law, banning horse-drawn carriages and phasing the industry out by June 1, 2028, by a vote of 40 to 7 with two abstentions.
  • The law honours Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old from Pathankot, who died in June after diving to save his mother, Priya, when their carriage horse bolted in Central Park.
  • The package includes a worker transition programme — job referrals, career counselling, hiring fairs and compensation for owners — and a rule that retired horses must not be sold for slaughter, with certification required by June 1, 2027.
  • The bill goes to Mayor Zohran Mamdani, but passed with a veto-proof majority; the carriage drivers' union says it will seek court orders against it.

The New York City Council has passed a law banning horse-drawn carriages and named it in honour of an Indian teenager killed in Central Park, according to IANS reporting carried by BizzBuzz. Romanch's Law was adopted on Thursday with 40 of the Council's 51 members in favour, seven against and two abstaining, The Hindu reported.

What Happened to Romanch Mahajan

Romanch Mahajan, 18, had just passed his higher secondary examinations at Angel's Public School in Mamun, Pathankot, and was visiting New York with his parents and brother. On June 17, the family was touring Central Park when the carriage driver stopped to take a photograph of them. The horse bolted, the carriage overturned, and Romanch's mother, Priya, was thrown from the vehicle. Romanch dove after her; his head struck the ground, and he died later in hospital.

https://x.com/the_hindu/status/2113624444258447618

His uncle, Gaurav Mahajan, addressed a rally of the ban's supporters outside City Hall before the vote.

"True justice means recognising that these gentle, majestic horses do not belong on the congested asphalt or trapped in dangerous traffic. On behalf of his parents and his brother, I leave New Yorkers with one final sacred request: please do not forget Romanch."

— Gaurav Mahajan, Romanch Mahajan's uncle

What the Law Does

Romanch's Law phases out the horse-drawn carriage industry by June 1, 2028, ending the issuing of new licences and prohibiting the operation of horse-drawn cabs. It was first introduced by Council Member Christopher Marte — originally as Ryder's Law, after a carriage horse that collapsed and died in 2022 — championed by Council Speaker Julie Menin, and renamed for Romanch after his death, which Menin marked by convening a Council hearing in July.

The phase-out is paired with protections on both sides of the trade. The city must develop a workforce transition plan — job referrals, career counselling, hiring fairs and compensation for business owners — and horse owners must certify by June 1, 2027 that no retired horse will be sold or transferred for slaughter or any inhumane purpose. PETA has offered $50,000 to help retire horses to rescue farms.

Menin called the vote "a demonstration of this Council's commitment to animal welfare, public safety, and worker protection." The bill now goes to Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who backed ending the industry; even a refusal to sign would not stop it, given the veto-proof margin.

The Opposition

The ban ends a tourist tradition of roughly 160 years, and its opponents were explicit about the cost. The Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage owners and drivers, said it will seek temporary restraining orders in court, arguing the law deprives owners of their livelihoods. Medet Fidan, who has driven a carriage for 15 years after ride-share apps upended his taxi work, said: "We're going to lose our businesses, we're going to lose our jobs, we're going to lose our livelihoods." President Donald Trump also criticised the ban on social media, questioning why carriages were being banned while cars remain permitted.

Animal-welfare campaigners had sought a ban since at least 2007 and were repeatedly blocked by the industry. What changed, by the Council's own account, was Romanch's death — which moved the argument from animal welfare alone to public safety on congested city streets.

What Happens Next

The transition plan is due first, with the slaughter-certification deadline on June 1, 2027 and the full phase-out on June 1, 2028, unless the union's court challenge intervenes. For the Mahajan family, the outcome is already fixed in one respect: the name on the law is their son's.
